title: Peter's Defense and the Church at Antioch
summary: Believers in Jerusalem criticize Peter for eating with uncircumcised men, and he answers by retelling what happened at Caesarea; they fall silent and praise God for granting the Gentiles repentance unto life. Meanwhile, scattered believers from Cyprus and Cyrene preach to Greeks in Antioch, and a large mixed church forms there. Barnabas and Saul teach it for a year, the disciples are first called Christians, and the church sends famine relief to Judea.
story: Chapter 10 opened the door to the Gentiles in one household. This chapter shows the church deciding whether to walk through it. First the Jerusalem believers test Peter's conduct and accept God's verdict. Then Luke rewinds to the persecution after Stephen's death (8:1-4) and follows another thread: unnamed believers who, apparently without any apostle's direction, begin telling Greeks in Antioch about Jesus. Antioch becomes the first great church with Gentiles in large numbers, and it will be the base for Paul's missions (13:1-3). By the end of the chapter Barnabas and Saul, who will lead the next stage of the story, are working side by side, and a church of Jews and Gentiles is caring for Jewish believers in Judea.
historical:
Antioch on the Orontes River (near modern Antakya in southern Turkey) was founded around 300 BC by Seleucus I, one of the successors of Alexander the Great, and was the capital of the Roman province of Syria. It was among the largest cities of the empire, usually ranked with Rome and Alexandria, and it had a large and long-established Jewish community. Tarsus, where Barnabas goes to find Saul, was Saul's home city in Cilicia, to the northwest across the mountains; Acts last left him there in 9:30. Phoenicia is the coastal strip of Tyre and Sidon, Cyprus the island off that coast (Barnabas's home, 4:36), and Cyrene a Greek city in North Africa, in modern Libya, with its own Jewish population.

Agabus predicts a famine over the whole world, and Luke notes that it happened under Claudius, emperor from AD 41 to 54. Ancient writers report a series of food shortages in various regions during his reign rather than one empire-wide famine at a single moment. The Jewish historian Josephus describes a severe famine in Judea in the mid-40s AD, when Helena, queen of Adiabene and a convert to Judaism, bought grain in Egypt for Jerusalem. The relief sent from Antioch fits that setting, though its exact year is uncertain.
cultural:
The criticism in verse 3 is not about theology in the abstract but about a meal: You visited uncircumcised men and ate with them. Table fellowship expressed belonging, and for many Jews sharing a table with Gentiles threatened purity and blurred Israel's distinct identity. That is why the question returns again and again in the early church (Galatians 2:11-14).

The name Christians (verse 26) is a Greek word formed with a Latin-style ending, -ianus, used for the followers or partisans of someone, as with the Herodians. It meant Christ's people. Believers in Acts call themselves disciples, brothers, saints, or followers of the Way, and the name Christian appears only three times in the New Testament (here, 26:28, and 1 Peter 4:16), each time on the lips of outsiders or in a setting of suffering. Most scholars think it was coined by outsiders in Antioch, who noticed that this group could no longer be described simply as a Jewish sect. The elders of verse 30 are the first mention of this office in the Jerusalem church: older, respected men who led the community, following the pattern of Jewish synagogues and towns.
literary: The chapter has two halves joined by the theme of the gospel crossing to Gentiles. In the first (verses 1-18), Peter retells chapter 10 in his own words and in order, a technique of repetition Luke uses for events he considers decisive (Paul's conversion is told three times). Peter adds details: six brothers went with him, and he remembered Jesus's promise about baptism with the Spirit. The section ends with the objectors silenced and praising God. The second half (verses 19-30) is a compressed report of growth, with short summary statements (a great number of people believed; a great number were brought to the Lord) and the introduction of characters Luke will need later: Barnabas, Saul, Agabus, and the elders. Verse 19 deliberately repeats the language of 8:4, telling the reader that this thread picks up where the story of scattering left off.

outline.t: Peter retells the events at Joppa and Caesarea
Repentance unto life for the Gentiles
The gospel reaches Greeks at Antioch
Barnabas and Saul teach the church; the name Christian
Agabus's prophecy and relief for Judea

doctrines.note: The Jerusalem believers conclude that God has granted even the Gentiles repentance unto life (verse 18). Repentance here is not a qualification Gentiles achieve but a gift God gives, a turning of the whole life that leads to life.

Antioch shows the church taking a new shape: Jews and Gentiles in one body, taught for a year by a Jewish teacher from Cyprus and a converted Pharisee from Tarsus, and generous to believers they have never met. Its unity is expressed in shared teaching and shared money.

Peter's decisive argument is that God gave the Gentiles the same gift of the Spirit he gave to Jewish believers. The Spirit's presence, not circumcision, is the mark that someone belongs to God's people.

words.note: Metanoia, repentance, literally a change of mind, but in the Bible a change of direction in the whole person, turning from sin and toward God. Luke uses the word often. Here it is paired with life: the turning God grants leads to the life of the age to come.

Christianos, Christian, one belonging to Christ. The word appears only three times in the New Testament. It shows that outsiders had begun to identify this group by its devotion to one figure, Christ, which is the Greek translation of the Hebrew Messiah, anointed one.

Parakaleo, to call alongside, and so to urge, encourage, or comfort. Barnabas's name was explained in 4:36 as son of encouragement, and here he lives up to it, urging the new believers to abide in the Lord with all their hearts.

Diakonia, service or ministry. It can describe the ministry of the word or, as here, practical relief sent to the needy. The same word covers both, which says something about how the early church understood serving.

christ: Peter's case rests on something Jesus himself said: John baptized with water, but you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit (verse 16, recalling 1:5). The coming of the Spirit on Gentiles is the risen Jesus keeping his own promise and extending it further than his disciples expected. The confession that won Antioch was simple: they were proclaiming the good news about the Lord Jesus (verse 20). To Greek listeners, Lord was the decisive title, placing Jesus above every lord and god they had known. And the name that stuck to the believers there was his, not theirs. The church at Antioch was identified from the start by whom it belonged to.
questions: The Jerusalem believers changed their minds when they heard what God had done. What would it take for you to change a firmly held conviction about who belongs?
The church at Antioch was started by believers whose names Luke does not record. What does that suggest about how the gospel usually spreads?
Antioch's first recorded act as a church was to give money to people it had never met. How does generosity express what a church believes?
